Pregnancy

Metoclopramide for nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

You have been given a prescription for metoclopramide, but you are worried about taking a medicine this early in pregnancy. The reason for treating the sickness matters, too. Tell your prescriber whether you can keep down water, meals and any other medicines you need. Those details help them decide whether a tablet is a practical option and how soon you need another assessment.

What metoclopramide may help with

Metoclopramide is a prescription medicine that can ease nausea and vomiting. It acts on signals involved in vomiting and can help the stomach empty. The aim during pregnancy is practical: being able to drink, eat or keep necessary medicine down. A useful update for the team is whether you can now finish a drink or manage a small meal, even if you still feel queasy.

Pregnancy sickness can happen at any time of day. Mild symptoms often improve as pregnancy progresses. More severe sickness can leave you dehydrated or unable to do ordinary activities. When this happens, waiting for a particular week of pregnancy to pass can leave you increasingly unwell. If vomiting starts later in pregnancy or is accompanied by abdominal pain, ask to be assessed for other causes.

Why your clinician may offer it after another medicine

There is more than one medicine for pregnancy sickness. A clinician may suggest metoclopramide when an earlier option has not helped enough or is unsuitable. One reason it is often tried later is the small risk of distressing involuntary movements. The choice also depends on what has worked before, any adverse reactions and what other medicines you take.

Bring the names and strengths of the medicines you have tried, including anything bought without a prescription. Mention a previous movement reaction to a medicine, Parkinson's disease or epilepsy. Some medicines and conditions change whether metoclopramide is suitable. If you are vomiting up regular treatment for another condition, contact the team promptly so that they can plan around that as well.

What pregnancy studies show

A Danish registry study compared 28,486 pregnancies with first-trimester metoclopramide exposure against 113,698 matched pregnancies without that exposure. Major birth defects were identified in about 25 per 1,000 births in the exposed group and 27 per 1,000 in the comparison group. Researchers found no evidence of an increase overall. The small numerical difference does not show that taking the medicine prevents birth defects.

The study also found no increased risk of miscarriage or stillbirth in its analyses. Registry comparisons are observational: they cannot prove zero risk, measure exactly what each person took or answer every question about rare outcomes. The results are reassuring if you took metoclopramide before knowing you were pregnant. Your clinician can consider your health, stage of pregnancy and the risks of leaving severe vomiting untreated.

Understanding a 10 mg label and the form you receive

A box marked 10 mg tells you the strength of a tablet. The instructions on your own prescription tell you how much to take, when you may take it and how long to use it. Ask the pharmacist to explain anything unclear, especially if a liquid replaces tablets. Write down when you last took it. Vomiting shortly afterward does not tell you how much was absorbed, so do not immediately repeat the dose or double up.

Metoclopramide can also be given by injection in a healthcare setting. If each sip comes back up, ask for an assessment instead of repeatedly trying another tablet. The team may check your hydration, offer fluids through a vein, or choose another way of giving anti-sickness medicine. Agree when to call back if you are still vomiting despite treatment.

Which symptoms could be a side effect?

Sleepiness, diarrhoea and a low mood can occur. If you feel sleepy, avoid driving or using machinery. Tell the prescriber if symptoms bother you, persist or affect your mood. Give the name of the medicine and the time symptoms began so the team can consider both the treatment and the pregnancy sickness itself.

An involuntary movement can start even after an early dose. Your eyes might pull upward, for example, or the jaw or neck muscles might go into spasm. Stop taking metoclopramide and get urgent medical advice if you develop uncontrolled movements or spasms. Get emergency help for difficulty breathing, swelling of the throat or tongue, or fever with severe muscle stiffness and confusion.

How to plan follow-up during pregnancy

Contact your pregnancy care team promptly if you cannot keep fluids or essential medicines down, pass very little or dark urine, feel faint or are losing weight. Tell them what you have actually managed to drink and when you last passed urine. Treatment for dehydration and a review of the anti-sickness plan can take place together.

Taking an anti-sickness medicine alone does not usually call for extra fetal scans. Persistent severe pregnancy sickness can lead the team to offer additional growth checks. If you are using metoclopramide close to delivery, tell the maternity team when you last took it. Product information advises avoiding use at the end of pregnancy when possible because a newborn movement reaction cannot be ruled out. If treatment is needed then, the team can arrange monitoring of the baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Compare the expected benefit of treatment with the effect vomiting is having on hydration and nutrition.

Ask the pharmacist to check the strength, form and instructions and review any other medicines you use.

Agree on follow-up if vomiting continues and know which movement symptoms need urgent advice.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the questions to ask when metoclopramide is offered for pregnancy nausea, including what your prescription means and when symptoms warrant reassessment.

When to seek help

Seek urgent medical advice if you cannot keep fluids down or develop involuntary movements after metoclopramide. Difficulty breathing, a swollen tongue or throat, or fever with severe stiffness and confusion requires emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Tell the prescriber whether you can keep down drinks and other essential medicines.
  • Large first-trimester studies have found no increase in major birth defects overall.
  • Use the instructions on your own prescription and ask what to do if you vomit after taking it.
  • Get urgent help for involuntary movements, muscle spasms or signs of significant dehydration.

Frequently asked questions

Can metoclopramide be used during pregnancy?

It can be prescribed when the expected benefit warrants it. The assessment includes how much the sickness is disrupting drinking and eating, the alternatives and any prior adverse reactions. Contact your clinician if you cannot keep fluids down.

What if I took it in the first trimester?

A large matched study found similar rates of major birth defects with and without early exposure. Tell your maternity team what and when you took. They can explain your routine pregnancy care and consider any other circumstances that might affect follow-up.

Is a 10 mg tablet the right amount for me?

The strength alone cannot answer that. Check the dose, interval and duration with the prescriber or pharmacist. Do not take someone else's tablets, add an extra dose after vomiting, or extend the course yourself.

Which side effects need urgent attention?

Uncontrolled movements, eyes moving involuntarily or spasm of the jaw or neck need urgent advice. Stop taking the medicine if these occur. Seek emergency help for a swollen throat or breathing difficulty, or for fever with marked stiffness and confusion.

What if I cannot keep the treatment down?

Contact the maternity or medical team promptly, especially if you are passing little urine or cannot retain liquids or essential medicine. An injection, fluid treatment or a different anti-sickness plan may be more appropriate than another oral dose.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
